ref: Leg. 4 (chapter only; neither Otto nor ANF has sub-sections)
greek: Ἡμῖν δέ, διαιροῦσιν ἀπὸ τῆς ὕλης τὸν θεόν, καὶ δεικνύουσιν ἕτερον μέν τι εἶναι τὴν ὕλην, ἄλλο δὲ τὸν θεὸν καὶ τὸ διὰ μέσου πολύ (τὸ μὲν γὰρ θεῖον ἀγένητον εἶναι καὶ ἀΐδιον, νῷ μόνῳ καὶ λόγῳ θεωρούμενον, τὴν δὲ ὕλην γεννητὴν καὶ φθαρτήν)
greek_edition: Otto, Athenagorae philosophi Atheniensis Opera (Corpus Apologetarum vol. 7), Jena: Mauke 1857; archive.org athenagoraephilo00athe (OCR text layer + page images at 300-600 dpi read by eye). Otto prints theta as a special glyph (OCR shows it as ϑ); transcribed here as θ; accents and breathings as printed; ἀΐδιον with diaeresis as printed. Printed page 20 (PDF p.104); line 10 ἀγένητον in main text (Otto's note on p.44 confirms he printed ἀγένητον against editions' ἀγέννητον).
english: “(for that the Deity is uncreated and eternal, to be beheld by the understanding and reason alone, while matter is created and perishable)” — the preceding clause: “we … distinguish God from matter, and teach that matter is one thing and God another”
page: Otto 1857 p.20 (Greek); ANF vol.2 p.130 (English, OCR-derived, unchecked on scan)
what_it_says: God is uncreated and eternal, known by mind and reason alone, while matter is created and perishable.
limits: Says nothing about Son or Spirit; the contrast is God versus matter, not a plurality within God. Arians can cite it for God's uncreatedness, which Nicene theology shares.

greek: Ἐπεὶ δὲ ὁ λόγος ἡμῶν ἕνα θεὸν ἄγει τὸν τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς ποιητήν, αὐτὸν μὲν οὐ γενόμενον (ὅτι τὸ ὂν οὐ γίνεται ἀλλὰ τὸ μὴ ὄν), πάντα δὲ διὰ τοῦ παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ λόγου πεποιηκότα, ἑκάτερα ἀλόγως πάσχομεν, καὶ κακῶς ἀγορευόμεθα καὶ διωκώμεθα.
greek_edition: Otto, Athenagorae philosophi Atheniensis Opera (Corpus Apologetarum vol. 7), Jena: Mauke 1857; archive.org athenagoraephilo00athe (OCR text layer + page images at 300-600 dpi read by eye). Otto prints theta as a special glyph (OCR shows it as ϑ); transcribed here as θ; accents and breathings as printed; ἀΐδιον with diaeresis as printed. Printed page 22 (PDF p.106); verified by zoomed image crop.
english: “…since our doctrine acknowledges one God, the Maker of this universe, who is Himself uncreated (for that which is does not come to be, but that which is not) but has made all things by the Logos which is from Him, we are treated unreasonably in both respects…”
page: Otto 1857 p.22 (Greek); ANF vol.2 p.131 (English, OCR-derived, unchecked on scan)
what_it_says: God, uncreated, made all things through a Logos that comes from Him.
limits: The Logos is 'from Him' (παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ) and is the agent of creation; the text does not say it is a person or the Son, and it names no Son here. Unitarians and Arians read it as a created or subordinate instrument, so the Greek is compatible with that reading.

greek: Ὁρᾷς τὸν ὑψοῦ τόνδ᾽ ἄπειρον αἰθέρα / καὶ γῆν περιξ ἔχοντ᾽ ὑγραῖς ἐν ἀγκάλαις; / τοῦτον νόμιζε Ζῆνα, τόνδ᾽ ἡγοῦ θεόν.
greek_edition: Otto, Athenagorae philosophi Atheniensis Opera (Corpus Apologetarum vol. 7), Jena: Mauke 1857; archive.org athenagoraephilo00athe (OCR text layer + page images at 300-600 dpi read by eye). Otto prints theta as a special glyph (OCR shows it as ϑ); transcribed here as θ; accents and breathings as printed; ἀΐδιον with diaeresis as printed. Printed page 24 (PDF p.108), quoting Euripides; first verse at p.22 (PDF p.106): “Ὤφελε δ᾽, εἴπερ ἐστ᾽ ἐν οὐρανῷ Ζεύς, μὴ τὸν αὐτὸν δυστυχῆ καθιστάναι.”
english: “Do you see on high him who, with humid arms, / Clasps both the boundless ether and the earth? / Him reckon Zeus, and him regard as God.” (ANF's first verse rendering: “If Zeus indeed does reign in heaven above, / He ought not on the righteous ills to send.”)
translator: B. P. Pratten (ANF 2); the ANF footnote in the Euripides passage is editorial
page: Otto 1857 p.24 (Greek); ANF vol.2 p.131 (English, OCR-derived, unchecked on scan)
what_it_says: Athenagoras cites the poets (Euripides) to show that the one God who holds the cosmos is recognised beyond popular gods.
limits: Context only: a Euripidean fragment about a single high god, not Christian doctrine. The fragment number and Nauck edition were not checked. ANF's note says Athenagoras misread Euripides.

greek: Καὶ Φιλόλαος δέ, ὥσπερ ἐν φρουρᾷ πάντα ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ περιειλῆφθαι λέγων, καὶ τὸ ἕνα εἶναι καὶ τὸ ἀνωτέρω τῆς ὕλης δεικνύει.
greek_edition: Otto, Athenagorae philosophi Atheniensis Opera (Corpus Apologetarum vol. 7), Jena: Mauke 1857; archive.org athenagoraephilo00athe (OCR text layer + page images at 300-600 dpi read by eye). Otto prints theta as a special glyph (OCR shows it as ϑ); transcribed here as θ; accents and breathings as printed; ἀΐδιον with diaeresis as printed. Printed page 28 (PDF p.112).
english: “Philolaus, too, when he says that all things are included in God as in a stronghold, teaches that He is one, and that He is superior to matter.”
page: Otto 1857 p.28 (Greek); ANF vol.2 p.131 (English, OCR-derived, unchecked on scan)
what_it_says: Philolaus, like Athenagoras, taught that God is one and superior to matter.
limits: Shows the unity of God is a philosophical commonplace (Pythagorean). Says nothing about plurality in God.

greek: Εἰ τοίνυν οὐκ ἔστιν ἄθεος Πλάτων, ἕνα τὸν δημιουργὸν τῶν ὅλων νοῶν ἀγένητον θεόν, οὐδὲ ἡμεῖς ἄθεοι, ὑφ᾽ οὗ λόγῳ δεδημιούργηται καὶ τῷ παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ πνεύματι συνέχεται τὰ πάντα τούτον εἰδότες καὶ κρατοῦντες θεόν.
greek_edition: Otto, Athenagorae philosophi Atheniensis Opera (Corpus Apologetarum vol. 7), Jena: Mauke 1857; archive.org athenagoraephilo00athe (OCR text layer + page images at 300-600 dpi read by eye). Otto prints theta as a special glyph (OCR shows it as ϑ); transcribed here as θ; accents and breathings as printed; ἀΐδιον with diaeresis as printed. Printed page 30 (PDF p.114); ἀγένητον as printed (Otto's apparatus, note 11, says he kept it against editions' ἀγέννητον).
english: “If, therefore, Plato is not an atheist for conceiving of one uncreated God, the Framer of the universe, neither are we atheists who acknowledge and firmly hold that He is God who has framed all things by the Logos, and holds them in being by His Spirit.”
page: Otto 1857 p.30 (Greek); ANF vol.2 pp.131–132 (English, OCR-derived, unchecked on scan)
what_it_says: God framed all things by the Logos (dative with ὑφ᾽ οὗ, 'by whom') and holds them in being by His Spirit (τῷ παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ πνεύματι).
limits: Logos and Spirit are both 'from/of Him' and presented as God's agency (instrument, power). No hypostatic language, no 'person', no homoousios; the Logos is a dative of agency. Arians and Sabellians can both read it. ANF's 'by the Logos' adds nothing to the Greek.

greek: Οἱ δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς στοᾶς, … δι᾽ ἧς φασι τὸ πνεῦμα χωρεῖν τοῦ θεοῦ, πληθύνωσι τὸ θεῖον τοῖς ὀνόμασι, τῷ γοῦν ἔργῳ ἕνα νομίζουσι τὸν θεόν·
greek_edition: Otto, Athenagorae philosophi Atheniensis Opera (Corpus Apologetarum vol. 7), Jena: Mauke 1857; archive.org athenagoraephilo00athe (OCR text layer + page images at 300-600 dpi read by eye). Otto prints theta as a special glyph (OCR shows it as ϑ); transcribed here as θ; accents and breathings as printed; ἀΐδιον with diaeresis as printed. Printed page 32 (PDF p.116); the ellipsis omits καὶ ταῖς προσηγορίαις κατὰ τὰς παραλλάξεις τῆς ὕλης.
english: “…which they say is permeated by the Spirit of God, they multiply the Deity in name, yet in reality they consider God to be one.”
page: Otto 1857 p.32 (Greek); ANF vol.2 p.132 (English, OCR-derived, unchecked on scan)
what_it_says: Athenagoras reports the Stoics' view that a divine spirit (pneuma) pervades matter, and says they multiply God in name while in fact holding one God.
limits: Stoic 'Spirit of God' is material pneuma pervading the world; Athenagoras uses the phrase to contrast Stoic pantheism with his own doctrine. It does not show a personal Holy Spirit. Scholars differ on whether the Spirit here is the same concept as in Leg. 7 and 10.

greek: κινηθέντες μὲν κατὰ συμπάθειαν τῆς παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πνοῆς ὑπὸ τῆς αὑτοῦ αὐτοῦ ψυχῆς ἕκαστος ζητῆσαι, εἰ δυνατὸς εὑρεῖν καὶ νοῆσαι τὴν ἀλήθειαν
greek_edition: Otto, Athenagorae philosophi Atheniensis Opera (Corpus Apologetarum vol. 7), Jena: Mauke 1857; archive.org athenagoraephilo00athe (OCR text layer + page images at 300-600 dpi read by eye). Otto prints theta as a special glyph (OCR shows it as ϑ); transcribed here as θ; accents and breathings as printed; ἀΐδιον with diaeresis as printed. Printed page 34 (PDF p.118); read from the 200 dpi page image only (not zoomed); 'αὑτοῦ αὐτοῦ' as printed.
english: “…moved, by reason of their affinity with the afflatus from God, each one by his own soul, to try whether he could find out and apprehend the truth.”
page: Otto 1857 p.34 (Greek); ANF vol.2 p.132 (English, OCR-derived, unchecked on scan)
what_it_says: Poets and philosophers were stirred by a breath (πνοή) from God, but reached only conjecture.
limits: The word is πνοή ('breath'), not ἀπόρροια; ANF's 'afflatus' renders it. It describes a general divine breath in souls, not the Holy Spirit as a person. Sentence-internal text is in the PDF text layer as well.

greek: Ἡμεῖς δὲ ὧν νοοῦμεν καὶ πεπιστεύκαμεν ἔχομεν προφήτας μάρτυρας, οἳ πνεύματι ἐνθέῳ ἐκπεφωνήκασι καὶ περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ περὶ τῶν τοῦ θεοῦ. … ὡς ἔστιν ἄλογον παραλιπόντας πιστεύειν τῷ παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πνεύματι, ὡς ὄργανα κεκινηκότι τὰ τῶν προφητῶν στόματα, προσέχειν δόξαις ἀνθρωπίναις.
greek_edition: Otto, Athenagorae philosophi Atheniensis Opera (Corpus Apologetarum vol. 7), Jena: Mauke 1857; archive.org athenagoraephilo00athe (OCR text layer + page images at 300-600 dpi read by eye). Otto prints theta as a special glyph (OCR shows it as ϑ); transcribed here as θ; accents and breathings as printed; ἀΐδιον with diaeresis as printed. Printed page 36 (PDF p.120). First sentence verified by zoomed crop. Second sentence read at 200 dpi; OCR gives κεκινηκότῳ where the image reads κεκινηκότι.
english: “…we have for witnesses … prophets, men who have pronounced concerning God and the things of God, guided by the Spirit of God. … irrational for us to cease to believe in the Spirit from God, who moved the mouths of the prophets like musical instruments…”
page: Otto 1857 p.36 (Greek); ANF vol.2 pp.132–133 (English, OCR-derived, unchecked on scan)
what_it_says: The prophets spoke under a divine spirit (πνεῦμα ἔνθεον), and the Spirit from God moved their mouths as instruments.
limits: Greek has ὄργανα ('instruments') with no adjective; 'musical' is the translator's addition. 'Spirit' is not called a person. This is the mantic model (the Spirit operates on prophets as instruments), which Arians and Sabellians could each read either way.

greek: Οὐ γὰρ εἰ θεοὶ ὅμοιοι, ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι ἀγένητοι οὐχ ὅμοιοι· τὰ μὲν γὰρ γενητὰ ὅμοια τοῖς παραδείγμασι, τὰ δὲ ἀγένητα ἀνόμοια, οὔτε ἀπό τινος οὔτε πρός τινα γενόμενα. … ὁ δὲ θεὸς ἀγένητος καὶ ἀπαθὴς καὶ ἀδιαίρετος, οὐκ ἄρα συνεστὼς ἐκ μερῶν.
greek_edition: Otto, Athenagorae philosophi Atheniensis Opera (Corpus Apologetarum vol. 7), Jena: Mauke 1857; archive.org athenagoraephilo00athe (OCR text layer + page images at 300-600 dpi read by eye). Otto prints theta as a special glyph (OCR shows it as ϑ); transcribed here as θ; accents and breathings as printed; ἀΐδιον with diaeresis as printed. Printed page 38 (PDF p.122), zoomed crop verified for ἀγένητος καὶ ἀπα-(θὴς) and ἀδιαίρετος. The clause about Socrates (παρὸ γενητὸς, as read) is omitted and not relied on; the reading of its particle is uncertain.
english: “For not because they are gods are they alike, but because they are uncreated they are unlike… God is uncreated, and, impassible, and indivisible — does not, therefore, consist of parts.”
page: Otto 1857 p.38 (Greek); ANF vol.2 p.132 (English, OCR-derived, unchecked on scan)
what_it_says: God is uncreated, impassible and indivisible, and so not compounded of parts; uncreated beings cannot be alike.
limits: ἀπαθής and ἀδιαίρετος are the key attributes that Trinitarian writers had to reconcile with the Son and Spirit. The passage argues against plural gods, not for internal distinctions within God; Sabellians and Arians can both cite it.

greek: Ἐπεὶ δὲ αἱ φωναὶ τῶν προφητῶν πιστοῦσιν ἡμῶν τοὺς λογισμούς … οἳ κατ᾽ ἑκάστασιν τῶν ἐν αὐτοῖς λογισμῶν κινήσαντος αὐτοὺς τοῦ θείου πνεύματος ἃ ἐνηργοῦντο ἐξεφώνησαν, συγχρησαμένου τοῦ πνεύματος ὥσεὶ καὶ αὐλητὴς αὐλὸν ἐμπνεῦσαι), τί οὖν οὗτοι;
greek_edition: Otto, Athenagorae philosophi Atheniensis Opera (Corpus Apologetarum vol. 7), Jena: Mauke 1857; archive.org athenagoraephilo00athe (OCR text layer + page images at 300-600 dpi read by eye). Otto prints theta as a special glyph (OCR shows it as ϑ); transcribed here as θ; accents and breathings as printed; ἀΐδιον with diaeresis as printed. Printed page 42 (PDF p.126); flute clause verified by zoomed crop and PDF text layer.
english: “…who, lifted in ecstasy above the natural operations of their minds by the impulses of the Divine Spirit, uttered the things with which they were inspired, the Spirit making use of them as a flute-player breathes into a flute.”
page: Otto 1857 p.42 (Greek); ANF vol.2 p.133 (English, OCR-derived, unchecked on scan)
what_it_says: The prophets were moved by the divine Spirit as a flute-player breathes into a flute, and their words are therefore trustworthy witnesses.
limits: The image of the Spirit as breath in a pipe is a mechanical instrument model (ὡς / ὥσεὶ: 'as if'). It is the most used 'Spirit as instrument' text against personal-Spirit readings; a Trinitarian reply is that it is an analogy. It is not a claim that the Spirit is a power rather than a person; Athenagoras does not say.

ref: Leg. 9 (chapter only); the prophetic citations are ANF's references (Isa 44:6; 43:10–11; 66:1), not Athenagoras's
greek: Κύριος ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν· οὐ λογισθήσεται ἕτερος πρὸς αὐτόν. Καὶ πάλιν· Ἐγὼ θεὸς πρῶτος καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα, καὶ πλὴν ἐμοῦ οὐκ ἔστι θεός. Ὁμοίως· Ἔμπροσθεν ἐμοῦ οὐκ ἐγένετο ἄλλος θεὸς καὶ μετ᾽ ἐμὲ οὐκ ἔσται· ἐγὼ ὁ θεὸς καὶ οὐκ ἔστι πάρεξ ἐμοῦ.
greek_edition: Otto, Athenagorae philosophi Atheniensis Opera (Corpus Apologetarum vol. 7), Jena: Mauke 1857; archive.org athenagoraephilo00athe (OCR text layer + page images at 300-600 dpi read by eye). Otto prints theta as a special glyph (OCR shows it as ϑ); transcribed here as θ; accents and breathings as printed; ἀΐδιον with diaeresis as printed. Printed page 42 (PDF p.126) and p.44 (PDF p.128) for the last lines; first two sentences verified by zoom, rest read at 200 dpi.
english: “The Lord is our God; no other can be compared with Him. And again: I am God, the first and the last, and besides Me there is no God. … Before Me there was no other God, and after Me there shall be none; I am God, and there is none besides Me.”
page: Otto 1857 pp.42–44 (Greek); ANF vol.2 p.133 (English, OCR-derived, unchecked on scan)
what_it_says: Athenagoras quotes Old Testament statements that God alone is God and that there is no other God before or after him.
limits: Strict monotheism from Isaiah. The Greek shows the Lord (Κύριος) is God, with no Christ named. Trinitarian writers read these texts with the Logos or Son; Athenagoras does not. Unitarians cite this passage as they stand. The LXX identity of the Greek was not checked against a LXX text.

ref: Leg. 10 (opening sentence; listed because it states the 'one God' formula of A1's item 4)
greek: Τὸ μὲν οὖν ἄθεοι μὴ εἶναι, ἕνα τὸν ἀγένητον καὶ ἀΐδιον καὶ ἀόρατον καὶ ἀπαθῆ καὶ ἀκατάληπτον καὶ ἀχώρητον, νῷ μόνῳ καὶ λόγῳ καταλαμβανόμενον, φωτὶ καὶ κάλλει καὶ πνεύματι καὶ δυνάμει ἀνεκδιηγήτῳ περιεχόμενον, ὑφ᾽ οὗ γέγενηται τὸ πᾶν διὰ τοῦ αὐτοῦ λόγου καὶ διακοσμεῖται καὶ συγκρατεῖται, θεὸν ἄγοντες, ἱκανῶς μοι δέδεικται.
greek_edition: Otto, Athenagorae philosophi Atheniensis Opera (Corpus Apologetarum vol. 7), Jena: Mauke 1857; archive.org athenagoraephilo00athe (OCR text layer + page images at 300-600 dpi read by eye). Otto prints theta as a special glyph (OCR shows it as ϑ); transcribed here as θ; accents and breathings as printed; ἀΐδιον with diaeresis as printed. Printed page 44 (PDF p.128). Verb διακοσμεῖται as read on the page image; the PDF text layer gives διακεκόσμηται. Otto's apparatus notes διὰ τοῦ αὐτοῦ λόγου variant (Bodl. 1.2 δι᾽ αὐτοῦ λόγου).
english: “…we acknowledge one God, uncreated, eternal, invisible, impassible, incomprehensible, illimitable, who is apprehended by the understanding only and the reason, who is encompassed by light, and beauty, and spirit, and power ineffable, by whom the universe has been created through His Logos, and set in order, and is kept in being — I have sufficiently demonstrated.”
page: Otto 1857 p.44 (Greek); ANF vol.2 p.133 (English, OCR-derived, unchecked on scan)
what_it_says: Athenagoras lists God's attributes (uncreated, eternal, invisible, impassible, incomprehensible) and says the universe was made and held together through God's Logos.
limits: Appears in ch. 10, which is outside A1's assigned range: it is included because it states A1's 'one God' formula. Πνεύματι here is a 'spirit' surrounding God (dative among light and beauty), not a person. The Logos is the same Logos of ch.4 and 6. The rest of ch.10 belongs to another item.

ref: Leg. 10 (opening; cross-reference for the Son, belongs to another assignment)
greek: Νοοῦμεν γὰρ καὶ υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ. Καὶ μή μοι γελοῖόν τις νομίσῃ τὸ υἱὸν εἶναι τῷ θεῷ. Οὐ γὰρ ὡς ποιηταὶ μυθοποιοῦσιν, οὐδὲν βελτίους τῶν ἀνθρώπων δεικνύντες τοὺς θεούς, ἢ περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς ἢ περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ πεφρονήκαμεν.
greek_edition: Otto, Athenagorae philosophi Atheniensis Opera (Corpus Apologetarum vol. 7), Jena: Mauke 1857; archive.org athenagoraephilo00athe (OCR text layer + page images at 300-600 dpi read by eye). Otto prints theta as a special glyph (OCR shows it as ϑ); transcribed here as θ; accents and breathings as printed; ἀΐδιον with diaeresis as printed. Printed page 44 (PDF p.128); verified visually.
english: “…for we acknowledge also a Son of God. Nor let any one think it ridiculous that God should have a Son. For though the poets, in their fictions, represent the gods as no better than men, our mode of thinking is not the same as theirs, concerning either God the Father or the Son.”
page: Otto 1857 p.44 (Greek); ANF vol.2 p.133 (English, OCR-derived, unchecked on scan)
what_it_says: Athenagoras explicitly acknowledges a Son of God.
limits: Cross-reference only; the Son is treated in the ch.10 items of another assignment. Υἱός is not elsewhere in ch.1–9. Words 'ἀγένητον καὶ ἀΐδιον' occur in ch.4 and 10, so the Son is named in the same chapter as the uncreated God but no Son is explained here.
